idiom_name: value semantics plus compiler escape analysis (small values stay inside the struct, no per-instance allocation)
implementation_notes: Go has no union and no way to declare an inline buffer with a runtime choice, but it answers the underlying question with a different mechanism: composite values are stored inline in their containing struct or slice, and the FAQ records that 'a basic escape analysis recognizes some cases when such variables will not live past the return from the function and can reside on the stack'. That is the replacement for the classic structure - keep small records by value, put them in arrays and structs rather than behind pointers and interfaces (both of which force the value onto the heap), and reuse growable buffers per worker (a scratch slice, or sync.Pool for shared pools) instead of allocating per call. A hand-written generic inline-capacity container (a struct with an inline [N]T plus an overflow slice, no unsafe required and GC-safe) is legal, but it pays the inline capacity even when every value spills, so write one only after the profile demands it; the standard library itself favours value types and buffer reuse over in-object buffers.
pitfalls: Pointer and interface indirection defeats it: taking the address of a small value, storing it in an interface, or capturing it in a heap-allocated closure makes it escape, and Go then allocates it - keep hot small values inside structs and arrays, and pass them by value.

A slice header is copied, not its elements: reusing one scratch buffer across goroutines needs an explicit pool or a per-worker instance, and because an inline array inside a struct is copied with the struct, passing a big value type through a call chain can cost a full memcpy.

A hand-rolled inline/overflow representation has no destructor to lean on: the zero value must already be a valid empty representation and the invariant (length never exceeds the inline capacity) must hold for every method; the garbage collector scans inline arrays, so there is no reason to reach for unsafe tricks.
sources: The Go Programming Language FAQ, 'How do I know whether a variable is allocated on the heap or the stack?' - 'a basic escape analysis recognizes some cases when such variables will not live past the return from the function and can reside on the stack': https://go.dev/doc/faq#stack_or_heap
